articles.title: Que horas sai o resultado das eleições? | G1
articles.standfirst: Disputa entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro chega ao fim neste domingo (25), e eleitores poderão acompanhar em tempo real a apuração dos votos em todo o país pelo g1.
articles.summary: Disputa entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro chega ao fim neste domingo (25), e eleitores poderão acompanhar em tempo real a apuração dos votos em todo o país pelo g1.
articles.body:
Urna eletrônica. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

A votação do segundo turno das Eleições 2026 foi prorrogada por duas horas neste domingo (25) . Com a mudança, o fechamento das urnas, inicialmente previsto para as 17h, passou para as 19h (horário de Brasília), adiando o início da divulgação dos resultados da disputa entre Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) . Mas, afinal, que horas será conhecido o próximo presidente da República?

A partir desse horário, o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) começa a divulgar os primeiros resultados, que podem ser acompanhados em tempo real pelo g1 .

Apesar de a divulgação começar às 19h, não existe um horário exato para a definição do vencedor. O resultado depende da velocidade da totalização dos votos e da diferença entre os candidatos.

Em 2022, para se ter uma ideia, o próprio TSE declarou a vitória de Lula às 20h09 da noite do domingo de eleição. O presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), ministro Kassio Nunes Marques, informou neste domingo (25) que as eleições estão dentro do esperado e estimou que o resultado deverá ser conhecido até 21h.

Além da disputa presidencial, eleitores de cinco estados e do Distrito Federal também vão escolher seus próximos governadores.

Que horas começa a apuração das Eleições 2026?

De acordo com o TSE, a divulgação dos resultados do segundo turno começa a partir das 17h (horário de Brasília), quando está previsto o encerramento da votação em todo o país.

O horário é o mesmo para todos os estados, independentemente do fuso horário local. Isso acontece porque a Justiça Eleitoral utiliza o horário de Brasília como referência para a abertura e o fechamento das seções eleitorais.

A votação começa às 8h e termina às 17h, pelo horário de Brasília. No entanto, eleitores que ainda estiverem na fila no momento do encerramento poderão votar normalmente.

Quando será anunciado o próximo presidente?

Não há um horário previamente definido para o anúncio do vencedor da eleição presidencial.

A Justiça Eleitoral atualiza os resultados à medida que recebe e processa os boletins de urna enviados pelas seções eleitorais de todo o país.

Por isso, a definição do próximo presidente pode ocorrer antes mesmo de 100% das urnas serem totalizadas, quando a diferença entre os candidatos for matematicamente irreversível.

Como acompanhar o resultado das Eleições 2026 ao vivo?

Assim que a votação for encerrada, às 17h (horário de Brasília), e os primeiros dados começarem a ser divulgados, o eleitor poderá acompanhar ao vivo a apuração dos votos pelo g1.

articles.title: Extensão do horário de votação em MG e RS é solicitada ao TSE | G1
articles.standfirst: Pedido é para que os eleitores dessas localidades possam votar até as 19h, no horário de Brasília. Pelas regras atuais, a votação do segundo turno começou às 8h e termina às 17h.
articles.summary: A campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro solicitou ao TSE a extensão do horário de votação até as 19h em cidades de MG e RS afetadas por chuvas e falta de energia.
articles.body:
A campanha do candidato à Presidência da República Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) pediu neste domingo (25) ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) que prorrogue por duas horas o horário de votação, marcada para encerrar às 17h, em municípios de Minas Gerais, Rio Grande do Sul, Paraná, Santa Catarina e São Paulo.

O pedido é para que os eleitores dessas localidades possam votar até as 19h, no horário de Brasília. Pelas regras atuais, a votação do segundo turno começou às 8h e terminaria às 17h.

A campanha pediu que a extensão fosse aplicada em:

Minas Gerais: Belo Horizonte, Poços de Caldas e municípios da Região Metropolitana de Belo Horizonte que tenham locais de votação sem energia elétrica;

Rio Grande do Sul: São Borja, Itaqui e Uruguaiana, atingidas por chuvas e pela cheia do rio Uruguai.

São Paulo: São Paulo (capital), Jundiaí, Itapevi, Americana, Santa Bárbara d'Oeste, Itapetininga, Botucatu, Apiaí, Ribeira e Iporanga;

Santa Catarina: Tijucas, Videira, Trombudo Central, Joaçaba e Águas de Chapecó; com a distribuição de senhas, às 19h, aos eleitores presentes.

Segundo a petição apresentada ao TSE, as chuvas provocaram alagamentos, interrupções no fornecimento de energia e dificuldades de deslocamento durante a votação.

A campanha argumenta que essas condições podem impedir eleitores de chegar às seções eleitorais dentro do horário previsto.

O documento afirma que dados preliminares da Cemig apontaram que ao menos 163 locais de votação ficaram sem energia em Minas Gerais, sendo 18 em Belo Horizonte e 65 na Região Metropolitana. A petição também relata alagamentos na capital mineira e em Poços de Caldas.

No Rio Grande do Sul, a campanha cita aviso da Defesa Civil estadual sobre risco de inundação no Rio Uruguai entre São Borja e Uruguaiana, além de alerta hidrológico para São Borja.

Caso o TSE não aceite a prorrogação para todos os municípios indicados, a campanha pede, de forma alternativa, que as duas horas adicionais sejam concedidas pelo menos nos 163 locais de votação de Minas Gerais que teriam registrado falta de energia, além de locais específicos de Belo Horizonte e seções eleitorais de São Borja, Itaqui e Uruguaiana situadas em áreas sujeitas à cheia do Rio Uruguai.

A defesa de Flávio Bolsonaro também solicita que, se a prorrogação nesses moldes for considerada inviável, os juízes eleitorais de Minas Gerais e do Rio Grande do Sul sejam autorizados a estender a votação por até duas horas nas seções em que forem constatados problemas de acesso provocados por alagamento, interdição de vias, deslizamento ou falta de energia.

O pedido prevê ainda a possibilidade de extensão da medida a outros municípios, zonas e seções eleitorais que os tribunais regionais dos dois estados identifiquem como atingidos pelos problemas relacionados às chuvas.

Se a extensão for autorizada, a campanha pede ao TSE que a divulgação dos resultados da eleição presidencial comece somente depois do encerramento da votação nos locais abrangidos pela medida.

A petição afirma, no entanto, que a recepção e a totalização dos boletins das demais seções eleitorais poderiam continuar normalmente.

A campanha também pede que, independentemente da decisão sobre a extensão do horário, a Justiça Eleitoral considere como justa causa a ausência dos eleitores que não conseguirem comparecer por causa dos eventos climáticos deste domingo.

O processo foi apresentado ao TSE como pedido de providências e encaminhado à Presidência da Corte, ocupada pelo ministro Kassio Nunes Marques. A campanha pede uma decisão imediata, sob o argumento de que a solicitação perderá a finalidade depois do encerramento da votação.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: quem precisa assinar o caderno de votação? | G1
articles.standfirst: Eleitores com biometria reconhecida na urna não precisam assinar o caderno de votação; assinatura é obrigatória quando não há cadastro biométrico ou o reconhecimento falha.
articles.summary: Eleitores com biometria reconhecida na urna não precisam assinar o caderno de votação; assinatura é obrigatória quando não há cadastro biométrico ou o reconhecimento falha.
articles.body:
Nas Eleições 2026 , a necessidade de assinar o caderno de votação na seção eleitoral depende da identificação biométrica do eleitor. Segundo o TSE ( Tribunal Superior Eleitoral ):

Quando a biometria é reconhecida na urna, não é necessário assinar o documento.

Já nos casos em que o eleitor não tem a biometria cadastrada ou o reconhecimento não é realizado, a assinatura é obrigatória.

O segundo turno acontece neste domingo (25). Eleitores devem votar entre Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Lula (PT) como próximo presidente do Brasil.

O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) publicou uma nota, neste domingo (25), alertando para mensagens falsas que circulam nas redes sociais com orientações incorretas sobre "o que fazer caso um eleitor chegue à seção eleitoral e seja informado de que outra pessoa já votou em seu lugar".

🚨De acordo com o TSE, se uma pessoa comparecer para votar e descobrir que seu voto já consta como registrado, o presidente da mesa deve comunicar o caso ao juiz eleitoral, que tomará as providências cabíveis.

Embora haja a importância de comunicar o fato ao juiz eleitoral, não há fundamento para afirmar que o eleitor precisa cumprir uma sequência de providências em 15 minutos, exigir uma frase específica na ata ou registrar boletim de ocorrência no mesmo dia para que o caso possa ser apurado.

Também é falsa a informação de que o eleitor precisa obter imediatamente uma declaração de comparecimento sem voto para evitar multa.

Nesse caso, a pessoa constará como tendo votado e estará quite com suas obrigações eleitorais.

O que fazer caso você seja informado de que já votou?

Se a eleitora ou o eleitor comparecer à seção eleitoral e for informado de que consta como já tendo votado, embora não tenha exercido o voto, o caso será comunicado pelo presidente da mesa receptora ao juiz eleitoral para a adoção das providências cabíveis.

A pessoa não poderá votar novamente, uma vez que a urna já registrou o exercício do voto em seu nome.

O fato de uma pessoa ter votado no lugar da outra não presume crime eleitoral. Apenas com a investigação é que será confirmado o que ocorreu.

Todas as ocorrências registradas na seção eleitoral devem constar na ata . Além disso, não existe uma frase específica que o eleitor precise exigir que seja incluída no documento.

O tribunal também esclarece que não é permitido fotografar o Caderno de Votação , pois ele contém dados pessoais de outros eleitores.

articles.title: Lula é reeleito: quando será a posse presidencial em 2027? Veja a nova data | G1
articles.standfirst: Mudança aprovada em 2021 alterou a data da posse presidencial, que antes era realizada em 1º de janeiro. Nova regra será aplicada pela primeira vez em 2027.
articles.summary: Mudança aprovada em 2021 alterou a data da posse presidencial, que antes era realizada em 1º de janeiro. Nova regra será aplicada pela primeira vez em 2027.
articles.body:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) venceu o segundo turno das Eleições 2026 neste domingo (25) e foi reeleito presidente da República, derrotando Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) . Com a vitória, o petista garantiu mais quatro anos à frente do Palácio do Planalto e tomará posse em 5 de janeiro de 2027, conforme a nova regra estabelecida pela Constituição Federal.

O candidato eleito presidente da República no segundo turno das eleições 2026 tomará posse em 5 de janeiro de 2027. A cerimônia marca o início do novo mandato presidencial, que terá duração de quatro anos, até janeiro de 2031.

Quando é a posse dos governadores em 2027?

Já os governadores eleitos nos 26 estados e no Distrito Federal tomam posse no dia seguinte, 6 de janeiro de 2027. Assim como o presidente da República, os governadores têm mandatos de quatro anos.

Por que a data da posse presidencial mudou?

As datas foram alteradas pela Emenda Constitucional nº 111, aprovada em setembro de 2021. Antes da mudança, as cerimônias eram realizadas em 1º de janeiro.

Esta será a primeira vez que a nova regra será aplicada às posses presidencial e dos governadores. Isso porque, embora a mudança tenha sido aprovada em 2021, as novas datas só passaram a valer para os eleitos a partir de 2026. Por isso, a posse de Lula em 2023 ainda ocorreu em 1º de janeiro.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: Apuração é pausada após Zanin prorrogar votação | G1
articles.standfirst: Cristiano Zanin, do STF, prorrogou a votação até as 19h em todo o país. Campanhas de Lula e Flávio pediram prorrogação por falhas no transporte público e chuvas, respectivamente.
articles.summary: O ministro Cristiano Zanin prorrogou a votação das Eleições 2026 até as 19h após pedidos das campanhas de Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro, pausando a apuração do TSE.
articles.body:
A última atualização no sistema do TSE, realizada às 17h06, mostra que 1225 seções eleitorais em todo o Brasil tiveram os votos para presidente apurados.

O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) aparece com 57,66%, com 193.574 votos. O senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) aparece com 42,34%, com 142.169 votos.

"Considerando a gravidade dos fatos narrados, que chegaram ao conhecimento do Supremo Tribunal Federal em 16:32:49, da data de hoje, e diante da urgência evidente na medida, determino prorrogação por duas horas, até às 19h, horário de Brasília, do encerramento do recebimento dos votos em todas as seções de todo o Brasil, cabendo ao TSE dar cumprimento", afirmou Zanin.

A medida abrangia pelo menos nove estados: São Paulo, Alagoas, Pernambuco, Roraima, Piauí, Paraíba, Pará, Paraná e Rio de Janeiro.

O documento é desdobramento de um outro pedido feito no início da tarde para três municípios baianos: Salvador, Feira de Santana e Lauro de Freitas.

A campanha também protocolou o pedido no Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ). O ministro Cristiano Zanin foi sorteado relator do pedido no STF.

Os advogados da campanha de Lula dizem que relatos de falhas no transporte de eleitores se multiplicaram ao longo do dia por diversas regiões do país.

De acordo com a petição, eleitores que dependem do transporte coletivo enfrentaram dificuldades para chegar aos seus locais de votação.

Urna eletrônica tem as teclas '2' e '3' coladas e é trocada em Gravataí — Foto: TSE/Divulgação

Entre as principais irregularidades descritas no pedido ao TSE constam:

São Paulo: o pedido aponta que, mesmo com determinação judicial para 100% da frota na capital, cerca de 60% dos veículos estariam circulando, com poucos ônibus no Centro, Zona Leste e Avenida Paulista.

Alagoas: falta de transporte complementar intermunicipal, vans e micro-ônibus, com filas superiores a uma hora e denúncias de cobrança indevida de passagem a eleitores, o que demandou atuação do Ministério Público.

Pernambuco: relatos de dificuldades no acesso à gratuidade em ônibus intermunicipais.

Roraima: recusa de empresas contratadas em cumprir rotas eleitorais, prejudicando o deslocamento de comunidades indígenas.

Piauí e Paraíba: queixas de redução da frota em Teresina e vídeos em João Pessoa mostrando coletivos passando direto por pontos em uma região da cidade.

Rio de Janeiro e Pará: notificações de frota reduzida e longas esperas em Petrópolis e São Gonçalo (RJ). E dificuldades de deslocamento na região do Marajó (PA).

A coligação também pede a determinação à Polícia Federal e às demais autoridades policiais para efetuarem a prisão em flagrante de responsáveis "pelo embaraço" ao exercício do voto.

A Federação Brasil da Esperança também solicitou que os juízos eleitorais dos municípios determinem que, às 17h, distribuam senhas a todos os eleitores presentes nos locais de votação, inclusive nas áreas externas e no acesso ao prédio.

A campanha do candidato à Presidência da Repúblcia Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) pediu neste domingo (25) ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) que prorrogue por duas horas o horário de votação , marcada para encerrar às 17h, em municípios de Minas Gerais e do Rio Grande do Sul atingidos por fortes chuvas.

A campanha pede que a extensão seja aplicada em:

Minas Gerais: Belo Horizonte, Poços de Caldas e municípios da Região Metropolitana de Belo Horizonte que tenham locais de votação sem energia elétrica;

Rio Grande do Sul: São Borja, Itaqui e Uruguaiana, atingidas por chuvas e pela cheia do rio Uruguai.

articles.title: Quantas eleições Lula disputou e quantas venceu? Relembre | G1
articles.standfirst: Trajetória eleitoral do petista começou na década de 1980 e inclui disputas para o governo de São Paulo e para a Presidência da República.
articles.summary: Trajetória eleitoral do petista começou na década de 1980 e inclui disputas para o governo de São Paulo e para a Presidência da República.
articles.body:
Presidente Lula (PT) durante a sanção dos novos limites do MEI e envio de PEC sobre tarifa zero no transporte coletivo aos fins de semana e feriados, no Palácio do Planalto — Foto: Ricardo Stuckert

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) foi reeleito presidente da República neste domingo (25), após derrotar Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) no segundo turno das Eleições 2026 . Com a vitória, o petista conquistou seu quarto mandato presidencial, ampliando uma trajetória eleitoral que começou há mais de quatro décadas.

Mas, afinal, quantas eleições Lula disputou e quantas venceu?

Considerando todas as disputas eleitorais de sua carreira, Lula participou de nove eleições e venceu cinco, incluindo a vitória hipotética de 2026. Dessas disputas, oito foram para a Presidência da República e uma para o governo de São Paulo.

Na corrida presidencial, o petista foi derrotado três vezes consecutivas, em 1989, 1994 e 1998, antes de conquistar sua primeira vitória, em 2002.

Veja a trajetória eleitoral de Lula, desde sua primeira candidatura:

1982 — Governo de São Paulo: Lula disputou o cargo de governador pelo PT, mas foi derrotado por Franco Montoro (PMDB).

1989 — Presidência da República: disputou sua primeira eleição presidencial e perdeu no segundo turno para Fernando Collor de Mello.

1994 — Presidência da República: foi derrotado por Fernando Henrique Cardoso (PSDB), que venceu no primeiro turno.

1998 — Presidência da República: voltou a enfrentar Fernando Henrique Cardoso e perdeu novamente no primeiro turno.

2002 — Presidência da República: conquistou sua primeira vitória presidencial ao derrotar José Serra (PSDB) no segundo turno.

2006 — Presidência da República: foi reeleito após vencer Geraldo Alckmin (PSDB) no segundo turno.

2022 — Presidência da República: voltou ao Palácio do Planalto após derrotar Jair Bolsonaro (PL) no segundo turno.

2026 — Presidência da República: neste cenário hipotético, venceu Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) no segundo turno e conquistou seu quarto mandato.

Quantas vezes Lula foi eleito presidente?

Com a vitória considerada neste cenário, Lula foi eleito presidente quatro vezes: em 2002, 2006, 2022 e 2026.

O petista governou o Brasil entre 2003 e 2010, retornou à Presidência em 2023 e iniciará seu quarto mandato em 5 de janeiro de 2027.

Lula também se tornaria o primeiro presidente brasileiro a conquistar quatro mandatos pelo voto direto.

Sim. Antes de vencer pela primeira vez em 2002, Lula acumulou três derrotas consecutivas em eleições presidenciais.

A primeira aconteceu em 1989, quando perdeu para Fernando Collor de Mello no segundo turno. Em 1994 e 1998, foi derrotado por Fernando Henrique Cardoso, nas duas ocasiões ainda no primeiro turno.

Depois dessas derrotas, Lula venceu todas as eleições presidenciais que efetivamente disputou: 2002, 2006, 2022 e, neste cenário hipotético, 2026.

articles.title: Presidente do PT vê gravidade na falta de ônibus em SP e Salvador | G1
articles.standfirst: Avaliação dentro do partido é de que a redução da oferta de transporte pode comprometer a participação de eleitores, especialmente nas regiões mais populares das duas cidades.
articles.summary: Avaliação dentro do partido é de que a redução da oferta de transporte pode comprometer a participação de eleitores, especialmente nas regiões mais populares das duas cidades.
articles.body:
Ônibus são retidos em garagem de Salvador durante o 2º turno das eleições — Foto: Karol Moreira/Arquivo Pessoal

O presidente nacional do PT, Edinho Silva, classificou como “muito grave” a falta de ônibus em São Paulo e Salvador neste domingo (25), dia do segundo turno da eleição presidencial.

Na avaliação do dirigente, os problemas no transporte público penalizam principalmente a base eleitoral do presidente Lula, formada também por eleitores que dependem dos ônibus para chegar aos locais de votação.

Diante da situação, o PT defende a prorrogação do horário de votação para garantir que os eleitores afetados pelas dificuldades de deslocamento possam exercer o direito ao voto.

A avaliação dentro do partido é de que a redução da oferta de transporte pode comprometer a participação de eleitores, especialmente nas regiões mais populares das duas cidades.

O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) cobrou explicações urgentes do Tribunal Regional Eleitoral da Bahia (TRE-BA ) sobre a redução ou interrupção do transporte público em Salvador, Feira de Santana e Lauro de Freitas durante o segundo turno das eleições presidenciais, neste domingo (25).

Em São Paulo, O Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT) denunciou à Justiça Eleitoral que a Prefeitura de São Paulo estaria operando com apenas 60% da frota de ônibus neste domingo. A denúncia ocorre em meio a relatos de passageiros sobre longas esperas nos pontos de ônibus e dificuldades para utilizar o transporte público em diferentes regiões da capital.

articles.title: Prorrogação do horário de votação: veja a cronologia | G1
articles.standfirst: Pleito foi extendido após determinação do ministro Cristiano Zanin, do Supremo Tribunal Federal.
articles.summary: A prorrogação do horário de votação foi determinada pelo ministro Cristiano Zanin após pedidos das campanhas sobre problemas no transporte e clima.
articles.body:
As campanhas de Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) acionaram o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) e o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) para tentar ampliar o horário de votação no segundo turno, neste domingo (25), após relatos de dificuldades enfrentadas por eleitores para chegar às seções eleitorais.

O ministro Cristiano Zanin, do STF, determinou a prorrogação da votação até as 19h em todo o país. A decisão, no entanto, foi divulgada pouco depois das 17h, quando parte das seções eleitorais já havia encerrado os trabalhos. Em alguns locais, as urnas já tinham sido fechadas ou até mesmo entregues à Justiça Eleitoral, o que impediu a aplicação da medida.

Às 17h49, o presidente do TSE, Kassio Nunes Marques, assinou um ofício orientando as seções eleitorais que ainda estavam abertas a permanecer em funcionamento até as 19h. Posteriormente, Zanin esclareceu que a prorrogação deveria valer apenas para as seções em que as urnas ainda estavam abertas no momento de sua primeira decisão.

13h22: Um pedido da campanha do PT é distribuído por sorteio no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE). O partido solicita a apuração de problemas na oferta de transporte público coletivo em Salvador, Feira de Santana e Lauro de Freitas, na Bahia. O caso chega ao gabinete do presidente da Corte, ministro Kassio Nunes Marques, às 13h54.

13h37: O PT também aciona a Corregedoria-Geral Eleitoral sobre os problemas no transporte público nos três municípios baianos. Às 14h31, o corregedor, ministro Ricardo Villas Bôas Cueva, determina que as presidências do TSE e do Tribunal Regional Eleitoral da Bahia (TRE-BA) sejam comunicadas e solicita informações ao tribunal regional sobre a situação.

Por volta das 15h: Advogados do PT solicitam a prorrogação do horário de votação em todo o país.

15h27: Um pedido da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) para ampliar o horário de votação é distribuído por sorteio no TSE. O partido aponta dificuldades enfrentadas por eleitores em municípios de São Paulo, Paraná e Santa Catarina devido a chuvas, alagamentos, deslizamentos e falta de energia . Minutos depois, o processo é encaminhado à presidência da Corte, ocupada por Nunes Marques.

15h46: O PT aciona o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) e pede a prorrogação da votação até as 19h em seções eleitorais de Salvador, Feira de Santana e Lauro de Freitas, sob o argumento de que problemas no transporte público prejudicavam o deslocamento dos eleitores.

16h29: O PT apresenta ao STF um novo pedido para estender a prorrogação do horário de votação a todo o território nacional.

16h33: O caso é distribuído ao ministro Cristiano Zanin, do STF.

articles.title: Lula é reeleito aos 80 anos e se torna novamente o presidente mais velho da história do Brasil; veja ranking | G1
articles.standfirst: Petista supera o próprio recorde de idade ao conquistar um quarto mandato presidencial; posse está prevista para janeiro de 2027.
articles.summary: Petista supera o próprio recorde de idade ao conquistar um quarto mandato presidencial; posse está prevista para janeiro de 2027.
articles.body:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) foi reeleito presidente da República neste domingo (25), após derrotar Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) no segundo turno das Eleições 2026 . Aos 80 anos, o petista se tornou o presidente mais velho a vencer uma eleição presidencial no Brasil e, em janeiro de 2027, assumirá seu quarto mandato aos 81 anos.

Com a vitória, Lula supera o próprio recorde. Até então, ele já era o presidente mais velho a tomar posse no país, ao assumir seu terceiro mandato em 1º de janeiro de 2023, aos 77 anos.

O presidente completará 81 anos em 27 de outubro de 2026, apenas dois dias após o segundo turno. A posse do novo mandato está marcada para 5 de janeiro de 2027.

Quem foram os presidentes mais velhos do Brasil?

Lula já ocupava o primeiro lugar entre os presidentes eleitos pelo voto direto mais velhos a assumir o cargo. Com a reeleição, ampliará esse recorde.

Veja alguns dos presidentes eleitos mais velhos na data da posse, considerando também mandatos de reeleição:

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva: 81 anos, em 2027.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva: 77 anos, em 2023.

Fernando Henrique Cardoso: 67 anos, em 1999.

A lista considera apenas presidentes que chegaram ao cargo por meio de eleições diretas. Por isso, não inclui Michel Temer, que assumiu a Presidência aos 75 anos, em 2016, após o impeachment de Dilma Rousseff.

Lula será o primeiro presidente a cumprir quatro mandatos?

Caso a reeleição seja confirmada, Lula será o primeiro presidente brasileiro eleito para quatro mandatos pelo voto direto.

O petista venceu as eleições presidenciais de 2002 e 2006, retornou ao Palácio do Planalto após vencer a disputa de 2022 e, neste cenário, conquistaria uma nova vitória em 2026.

O quarto mandato começará em 5 de janeiro de 2027 e terminará em 5 de janeiro de 2031, quando Lula terá 85 anos.

articles.title: Trump critic Lula wins reelection in Brazil, securing fourth presidential term
articles.summary: RIO DE JANEIRO (AP) — Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of U. President Donald Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that keeps...
articles.body:
Brazil's presidential runoff between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro, in photos

RIO DE JANEIRO (AP) — Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of U.S. President Donald Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that keeps some distance between Latin America's biggest economy and Washington.

With 100% of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon to be 81-year-old Lula held an unassailable lead. The announcement capped an evening of chaos at polling places across Brazil, following a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours. That decision by a Supreme Court justice may trigger legal action by opponent Flávio Bolsonaro.

His triumph bucks a trend in Latin America where increasing numbers of right-of-center presidental candidates allied with Trump have been winning, further extending the United States' influence in the region. Lula's victory leaves Mexico and Brazil, Latin America's two most populous nations, with left-of-center leaders. It also positions Latin America's largest economy, with a GDP of $2.6 trillion per year, to remain independent of the U.S., despite the pressure of increased tariffs imposed by Trump.

The announcement kicked off a celebration of supporters in and out the Sao Paulo hotel where Lula watched the count with First Lady Rosângela da Silva, allies, and friends.

Lula's victory, if confirmed by electoral authorities, will give him his non-consecutive fourth term as president. The next term begins on Jan. 5, 2027.

It is the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote getter in the first-round elections won the presidency. Bolsonaro had 47% of the vote in the first round to Lula's 45%, a difference of 2.2 million votes.

Lula and Sen. Bolsonaro have yet to address their supporters.

Sunday's victory will likely be the last of the veteran leader's political career. Lula began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader. He then helped found the Workers' Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times until he finally won it in 2002. He was reelected four years later and was succeeded by one of his cabinet ministers, Dilma Rousseff, in 2010. She was reelected in 2014.

Rousseff was impeached for accounting maneuvering in 2016 amid a sprawling corruption probe, which also ensnared Lula. He tried to run for president again in 2018 but was jailed in March after being convicted.

Lula was released from prison after 580 days and saw Brazil's Supreme Court annul his sentence after police found messages that showed the judge who convicted him was biased. He quickly became one of former President Jair Bolsonaro's biggest critics and narrowly beat him in 2022.

Lula admitted in 2024, two years into the job, that his administration had done little that far to earn the support of his voters.

Since he lost the first round, Lula reorganized his campaign, appealed to young voters, put millions of Brazilians on the streets to defend democratic values and his legacy, raised fears of another Bolsonaro administration and boosted several government initiatives.

Lula also defended Brazil's sovereignty and insisted that a Bolsonaro presidency would allow the U.S. to exert control over Brazil.

He joins Trump and Nicaragua's President Daniel Ortega — all age 80 — as the oldest presidents in the Americas.

Savarese reported from Sao Paulo. Brigida reported from Brasilia.

articles.title: Trump escalates anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed in Michigan, drawing Arab American rebuke
articles.summary: (AP) — President Donald Trump intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric against Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, portraying him as a threat to...
articles.body:
PORT HURON, Mich. (AP) — President Donald Trump intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric against Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, portraying him as a threat to national security and questioning his loyalty to the United States in remarks that drew a sharp rebuke from a former top Arab American ally.

Trump called El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official, a "jihadist" who was "on the side of the terrorists" and would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate." He also repeatedly invoked the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate chamber and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers aboard United Flight 93.

El-Sayed, who would become the nation's first Muslim senator if elected, has called attacks on his loyalty to the country "shameful" and repeatedly denied any ties to extremist groups. The Republican president's remarks were condemned by Bishara Bahbah, a founder of Arab Americans for Trump , the group that helped lead the president's outreach to Arab American voters in 2024.

"The president's statements are out of line," he said in a phone interview. "They are crossing a red line. They are racist."

With Republicans on the defensive over inflation, soaring fuel prices and the Iran war, the president has been trying to generate turnout by claiming that El-Sayed and other Democrats are existential threats to America, instead of electoral rivals. Michigan's Senate race between El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers is among a handful of contests that could determine control of the chamber.

Trump made his remarks in Port Huron, a Canadian border city about an hour north of Detroit and near communities where he made significant gains among Arab American voters in 2024. He became the first Republican presidential candidate since 2000 to win Dearborn , a city with one of the nation's largest concentrations of Arab Americans.

Trump, who imposed a travel ban targeting several predominantly Muslim countries during his first term, has increasingly leaned into anti-Muslim rhetoric as Election Day approaches. He also attacked Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota at Sunday's rally, where he declared that he had come to Michigan "to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator."

Cole Wozniak, a spokesperson for El-Sayed, responded to Trump's comments in a statement: "While they lie and resort to desperate, bad faith attacks, Abdul remains laser focused on his plans to bring down costs and stand up to the chaos and corruption in Washington."

El-Sayed's faith, associations and past statements become campaign flashpoints

Central to Republicans' strategy against El-Sayed in the final weeks of the campaign has been an effort to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamic movement with branches that the U.S. government has designated as terrorist organizations .

There is no evidence that El-Sayed has any affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood. His half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, wrote on social media in 2012 that "my family has long been MB" and described a conversation with her mother about her involvement in the Muslim Brotherhood in the early 1970s.

El-Sayed was born in the United States to Egyptian immigrant parents who divorced when he was young. He was raised by his father, not his biological mother.

Trump on Sunday also targeted El-Sayed's ties to popular streamer Hasan Piker, who appeared alongside the Democrat multiple times during the primary campaign, including at his election night event.

Piker in the past has said that "Hamas is a thousand times better" than Israel, describing some Orthodox Jews as "inbred" and that "America deserved 9/11."

El-Sayed has faced criticism for his own rhetoric. He has repeatedly refused to answer questions about whether Iran or Israel poses a bigger threat to the country. Earlier this year, he said "hurt people hurt people" after an attack on a synagogue in the Detroit area. The attacker had lost four relatives in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon the week earlier. El-Sayed later apologized , saying he was not trying to justify what happened.

"To anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful, I'm really sorry," he said. "That was not my intention."

Founder of Arab Americans for Trump calls the president 'racist'

Bahbah, whose organization has since changed its name to Arab Americans for Peace, said Trump's remarks were unacceptable to Arab and Muslim communities, including Christian Arabs.

"The remarks are out of line and crazy. I mean, no sane individual would say these things," Bahbah said.

Dearborn helped Trump win Michigan in 2024 after many voters in the city were outraged by the Biden administration's handling of the war in Gaza.

"The president of the United States saying that about a person because of his religion, that is just not acceptable," said Bahbah. "And people are going to remember that on Nov. 3."

The campaign has been one of the most contentious this year

Rogers and El-Sayed have been locked in a bitter race to fill the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

During their second and final general election campaign debate , Rogers questioned El-Sayed's loyalty to the United States.

"Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?" Rogers asked.

El-Sayed said that questioning was "shameful."

"I'm proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray," he said.

Speaking before Trump's appearance Sunday, Rogers repeated his allegations linking El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood.

"The Muslim Brotherhood celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year," Rogers said on stage. "Abdul El-Sayed's."

Rally doesn't deliver a new economic handout, but gets boost from Minaj

Trump has routinely announced new investments in factories at his campaign rallies, but he did not do so as part of his speech in Michigan, a state defined by the auto industry.

The president instead repeated investments already being made by domestic automakers. Those automakers could see their finances slump if the president expands his trade war with Canada, which has been an essential partner for the U.S. automotive sector.

While it lacked a fresh promise for Michigan's economy, Trump's rally did deliver a bit of star power.

Rapper Nicki Minaj appeared on stage and urged people to get out and vote for the state's Republican ticket. Her appearance followed an awkward moment from Trump, who has increasingly been fixated on commenting about other people's body parts.

After praising the body of Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican in a close election contest, Trump turned his eye toward Minaj and commented on her posterior.

The president then signaled for Minaj to stand for the crowd and she did, after which Trump said, "I hope Nicki wasn't insulted, but we love Nicki. She's been with us for a long time."

Cappelletti reported from Washington. Associated Press writer Josh Boak in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title: Democrat Scott Colom aims for deep-red Mississippi Senate seat
articles.summary: Colom would be Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.
articles.body:
Why are major Democrats and Republicans flocking to Mississippi in recent weeks?

In a climate where polls show President Donald Trump's approval ratings cratering, Democrats are unusually optimistic about Scott Colom's chances of flipping the Senate seat held by incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith -- even in deep-red Mississippi.

"We got to have a senator that looks out for Mississippi, that puts Mississippi farmers first, Mississippi small businesses first, represent our values by not allowing corruption to ruin our country and actually delivers on the commitments to put America first," Colom told ABC News in an interview earlier this week.

The incumbent's campaign dismisses the Democratic push as the last-ditch effort of a campaign that will fall short.

Colom is a district attorney for four counties along the Mississippi-Alabama border and a former nominee to become a U.S. district judge. He would be Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

Democrats have argued that Colom's prominent credentials, as well as voter pushback against Republican incumbents and motivation among Democratic-leaning Black voters, could help boost him. Mississippi's population is around 36% Black, according to U.S. Census data .

Colom faces an uphill battle, as Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1982 and voted for Donald Trump in 2024 by around 20 points. ABC News rates the race solid Republican.

But he has gotten the attention of national Democrats; major party figures such as former former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock have campaigned with him. Former President Barack Obama also recorded an ad for him released earlier this month.

Harris, during a rally with Colom on Thursday, told attendees, "I've been in those rooms where there's no cameras, it's senators talking to each other... When you have a voice like his in that room, just think about the impact that's going to have on the decisions coming out of that room. Think about that. This is no ordinary time, and this is no ordinary man."

Colom also went viral online last week after a social video he posted showed Hyde-Smith, during a local news interview from February, saying "You have so many proteins to choose from" while discussing how to deal with higher prices on meat and other goods. In the interview, Hyde-Smith also spoke about working on regulations that would help energy production, and tax incentives to help development.

But it was the proteins part that Colom's campaign seized on, with a punchy video that featured voters mocking the senator's words, with one saying, "Pick another protein ... I'd rather pick another Senator instead." (The campaign has confirmed to ABC News that the video has been turned into a campaign ad.)

One concrete sign of confidence among Democrats over Colom's chances came on Tuesday, when the Senate Majority PAC, an outside group aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, announced it would spend $1.2 million on an ad campaign across broadcast TV and digital for ads for Colom.

Asked what signs the group sees in Mississippi that makes it worth investing in, spokesperson Lauren French wrote, "Cindy Hyde-Smith has spent a decade in Washington without passing a single piece of legislation, and Mississippians have noticed."

Hyde-Smith has cosponsored legislation that has passed into law but legislation she initially sponsored or reintroduced has not become law, according to congressional records . Asked to respond to Senate Majority PAC, Hyde-Smith's campaign pointed to how bills from lawmakers "are often passed as part of larger legislative packages," and that has been true for some of Hyde-Smith's bills, including the first one she introduced. The campaign also pointed out that she is running for only her second full term.

French said Colom is running a "disciplined campaign" with messages resonating with voters.

Colom and Hyde-Smith have some history, as she blocked his nomination for federal judge in 2023. She cited his support for transgender rights and having previously been boosted by a George Soros-linked PAC, according to the Mississippi Free Press .

He insists his bid for Senate is not motivated by a desire to get back at her.

"It has nothing to do with the run for me ... as a Christian, I forgive her. It's about the people in Mississippi," Colom told ABC News.

"We are confident that Mississippians will once again send Cindy Hyde-Smith back to the U.S. Senate on November 3rd. This is simply Washington insiders making a last ditch effort to give life to Scott Colom's failing campaign," campaign manager Jake Monssen told ABC News in a statement.

Hyde-Smith's supporters may be more motivated after a boost from President Donald Trump, who's set to hold a rally in Mississippi on Monday as part of a swing of campaign rallies mostly in red states.

The Republican National Committee announced the rally around a week after Colom's social video went viral, although Trump and the group have not indicated why they are doing the rally there and Trump has expressed confidence in Hyde-Smith.

"Cindy Hyde-Smith's very popular ... So if I need to get her over the top, I would go there [to Mississippi]. She's great. Cindy Hyde-Smith is great," Trump told reporters when asked Thursday about the Senate election.

Hyde-Smith will be attending the rally, according to her campaign.

articles.title: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer says America is ready to elect a woman
articles.summary: The Michigan governor didn’t deny she’s exploring a run for president in 2028.
articles.body:
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer pushed back Sunday on comments made by former first lady Michelle Obama last year that U.S. voters aren't ready to elect a female president.

"Listen, I have got a lot of colleagues who I think are probably interested in running for president, and I've heard everyone say, 'You can't have this person or that person,'" the governor told NBC News' "Meet the Press."

"I would put my money on any Democratic governor in the country against [Vice President] JD Vance or [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio in 2028," she added, pointing to two Republicans widely expected to run for president in two years.

Asked directly whether a woman could be the best choice to beat a potential GOP presidential nominee in 2028, Whitmer simply said, "I do."

In 2025, Obama said in public remarks: "As we saw in this past election, sadly, we ain't ready. That's why I'm like, don't even look at me about running, because you all are lying. You're not ready for a woman. You are not."

Several women, including Whitmer and former Vice President Kamala Harris, are widely speculated to be potential candidates in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary.

On Sunday, Whitmer did not deny that she's exploring a potential run for president in 2028, saying that she'll decide on her next steps after she departs from her post as governor in January.

"When I exit office … I'm going to take a little time off and figure out what I want to do next, so I've got nothing new to share with you, unfortunately," Whitmer told "Meet the Press" moderator Kristen Welker.

Earlier this year, Whitmer denied that she planned to run for president but quickly walked back the comments.

"There will be a robust group of people running for president," she said at the time, adding, "I will not be one of them in 2028, I can tell you that."

Later the same day, the governor said: "I never thought I would run for governor. So I guess I should know better to never say never."

Several other Democratic governors, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, are also widely regarded as potential 2028 presidential candidates. Each has been crisscrossing the country ahead of the midterms campaigning on behalf of Democratic gubernatorial candidates in competitive races.

Whitmer on Sunday highlighted her support for former public health official Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor in Ohio.

Earlier this week, Acton's opponent, GOP businessman Vivek Ramaswamy, released a TV ad featuring Acton's mother calling her a "liar." Acton has publicly shared that she's been estranged from her mother for nearly 50 years and has accused her late stepfather of sexually abusing her. Acton and her brother were removed from her mother's custody in 1978 after her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested on a child rape charge. Acton's mother has not responded to requests for comment.

"I'm going to stay focused on getting people like Amy Acton over the finish line. What's happened to her in Ohio is absolutely abhorrent, and any survivor knows there's always a backlash. But this is what makes it harder for women to seek help after they've been sexually assaulted in this country," Whitmer said Sunday. "It is unreal what's going on, and that's why we've got to — we've got to win races like this and elect good people who are going to keep the people at the heart of their work, like Dr. Amy Acton."

Ramaswamy's decision to air the ad has faced widespread bipartisan condemnation , some of it from GOP Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio, who is locked in a tight re-election race.

articles.title: Blanche on Alaska suit: 'There could be a crime'
articles.summary: The attorney general took part in at-times contentious interviews on both CNN and CBS.
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday defended the Justice Department's newly filed lawsuit to prevent Alaska state officials from certifying election results if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses in November.

In an at-times contentious interview with CNN's "State of the Union," Blanche pointed out that according to the Constitution, Congress can create laws at any time to regulate elections. But when host Dana Bash asked what crime the administration was arguing was being committed, Blanche replied, "It depends."

"There could be a crime," said Blanche. "But the real wrong here is that Alaskans are going to be confused and will not have their vote heard. So an Alaskan intends to vote for one candidate, but is confused because of a second candidate with exactly the same name who has voted Democrat his entire life, who donated money to the other Democrat opponent, is running."

Bash pressed Blanche on how it is illegal for two candidates with the same name to be on a ballot at the same time.

"It is an obligation of the states to avoid confusion, among other things, confusion in the minds of voters in the election process," Blanche replied. "So the question is whether Alaska, by allowing this to happen, is violating the law and the federal law and the constitution by allowing confusion in the ballot."

The Alaskan Supreme Court in June ruled that both Sullivans may remain on the ballot as the incumbent faces off in a tight reelection battle with former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola. The four-person Senate ranked-choice ballot for the general election specifies that Dan S. Sullivan is a "Registered Republican" and the "incumbent" — no information is listed after Dan J. Sullivan Jr's name.

Regardless, in the suit filed Thursday , DOJ argued that Dan J. Sullivan Jr.'s name on the ballot constitutes a purposeful effort to mislead voters.

Still, it's unclear how much the court can do about the Justice Department's lawsuit. With ballots secret, it is virtually impossible for the Justice Department to identify specific voters and clarify which Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for.

Blanche, though, seemed unconcerned about that hurdle.

"There are a number of scenarios where it could be obvious that a voter was confused by the way they wrote down candidates," said Blanche.

President Donald Trump on Friday said the legal challenge was his idea, though Blanche on Sunday declined to state whether the president had directed him to file the suit.

"I will never talk about any communications I have with the president of the United States," he said.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who is not up for reelection this year, said Friday that the lawsuit is unnecessary.

"Alaskans don't need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year's ballot," Murkowski said in a post on X . "The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit."

Her comments drew the ire of Trump, who on Saturday called Murkowski "Republicans' Worst Senator, by far," in a post to Truth Social .

Trump said that Alaska's ranked choice voting system is "a TOTAL DEMOCRAT SCAM meant to confuse the Voter, so that Senator Dan Sullivan will lose Votes to a man who has never participated in Politics before, named Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr."

"He is only there because the Democrats want to steal the Election, and Murkowski probably wants that to happen, which is why she is against the DOJ filing a Lawsuit in order to stop this impending crime and tragedy," Trump added. "I have delivered for Alaska at Historic Levels, nobody has ever seen anything like it, and all I'm asking for is a FAIR AND HONEST SENATORIAL ELECTION! Lisa Murkowski is a DISGRACE to Alaska and our Country. You just don't get any worse!"

Democratic leaders have also widely condemned the lawsuit, arguing the president is attempting to lay the foundation to overturn the midterm election results if their candidates win critical elections — something Bash asked Blanche about on Sunday.

"One of the big questions is whether or not the president is laying the groundwork for a scenario where, whether it's Alaska or somewhere else, there is, in your words a couple of days ago, a 'doomsday scenario' and we could be in a situation where President Trump tries to overturn the election and the result of that could be, god forbid, what we saw after January 6th," Bash said.

Blanche quickly fired back: "Oh stop it. You gotta stop it with that. You're not being a real person. You set me up. You're saying, "'Mr. Attorney General, because the president of the United States wants to stop fraud and confusion in Alaska, is he going to do something crazy?' That is not a real question."

Bash replied that she did not think it was an unfair question, but Blanche argued that the premise of the question was untrue.

"Instead of focusing on how we can address that and how we can remedy that, you're talking about January 6th," he said. "That's so embarrassing to this network that that's what you're talking about."

"Don't "oh, come on" me," replied Blanche. "There's literally confusion."

It wasn't the only tense interview Blanche had Sunday.

In an appearance on CBS' "Face the Nation," Blanche accused host Margaret Brennan of lying over the wording of the Justice Department's lawsuit .

"The Alaska Supreme Court did take on this matter," Brennan began, referring to the court's June decision.

"No, they didn't. That's a state law," interrupted Blanche.

"In this country, the states administer the elections. This is how the state came up with the issue and how to handle any confusion," Brennan said as the Alaskan ballot was shown on the screen.

"You're not telling the truth," said Blanche.

Brennan asked why identifying Sullivan as the incumbent is insufficient for the administration.

"Well, listen, I don't know if it's sufficient," said Blanche. "But I can tell you this: that the director of the Alaska election system has said that it will likely cause confusion."

Brennan pointed out that the ballots are already circulating, and voting may already be underway, as many vote by mail in Alaska. She then pressed Blanche on Trump claiming responsibility for the lawsuit, to which Blanche reiterated that he will not share his communications with the president.

"The president of the United States said this on camera ," Brennan replied. "He said, "I told them to do it." Did he tell that to you?"

"He didn't say that on camera," argued Blanche, before adding Trump had been looking at the situation for "months and months and months." He later added that he had "no idea" who Trump was referring to, and even if he did, he would "most certainly not" talk about it.

Brennan then pivoted to read several lines from DOJ's lawsuit, including that the suit defined voter confusion as Sen. Sullivan not winning the election and that had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast for the incumbent then he would have won.

As she spoke, Blanche interrupted again.

"I'm quoting from it," Brennan replied, holding up a printed version of the suit. "You are telling them not to certify it. What right does the federal government have telling a state not to certify or how to certify?"

After a moment of crosstalk, Blanche stated: "If you talk the whole time you're not going to get answers out of me. If you let me answer your question I can address your question." He then said the suit does not call for officials to avoid certifying the election.

"All we're doing is trying to put guardrails in place so that if that happens there's a system allowed where the ballots are kept in a way so we can determine whether there was confusion," he explained.

In his interview with CNN, Blanche denied any political motivations were behind the Justice Department's lawsuit.

"It's important the American people understand that we are not — President Trump is not trying to take over a state election in any way, shape or form," he said. "What we're trying to do is make it clear that if it is obvious after the election, that confusion led to an improper and illegal result that the Alaskan system should be able to address that."

In an interview with NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday, Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) argued the administration has no standing to bring the Alaska lawsuit, and he lambasted Blanche for leading a "disgraceful campaign."

"This suit has no chance of succeeding," said Schiff. "But the fact that Todd Blanche and the Justice Department are willing to go along with it, they're willing to put their name on it, is an indication of how far they will go after this election is over to try to challenge the results."

articles.title: Libertarian Texas Senate candidate says he’s not taking votes away from Paxton, Talarico
articles.summary: Ted Brown, the Libertarian candidate in the highly contested Texas Senate race, shut down claims that votes for him could end up splitting votes, leading to...
articles.body:
Ted Brown, the Libertarian candidate in the highly contested Texas Senate race , shut down claims that votes for him could end up splitting votes, leading to a potential outcome that could cost Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) the election.

"Both sides are saying the same thing. Democrats are saying, hey, that I'm taking votes away from Talarico, and Republicans say I'm taking votes away from Paxton," Brown said in an interview with NewsNation's "The Hill Sunday."

"But in reality, I'm just promoting my candidacy and the Libertarian Party. We need an alternative in this party, in this country. And the two parties are just not providing it."

With the election less than two weeks away, Brown dismissed arguments that by voting Libertarian, the race would amount to handing control of the Senate to Democrats, saying his presence on the ballot offers voters a choice outside of the traditional two-party system.

"Every other aspect of life, there are multiple choices, paint colors, ice cream flavors, barbecue sauce, everything, except for politics. And it's very important. So I'm here to promote an alternative point of view," he said.

He continued, "I don't believe that votes for me are against the — they're for me and for an alternative, not to take down one of the major parties. Texas does have a Libertarian history, more within the Republican Party."

The dispute comes as Paxton, who was endorsed by President Trump in the primary, faces a competitive race against Democrat James Talarico for the seat held by Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas).

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report shifted the race in the deep red state from "likely red" to "toss-up," and several polls found Talarico with a slight lead ahead of Paxton in the last stretch of the race.

The narrow margin between the major party candidates has drawn attention to Brown's potential impact on the election.

articles.title: Mary Peltola delays campaign events after sustaining ‘minor injuries’ in car crash
articles.summary: Former Rep. Mary Peltola is rescheduling several upcoming campaign events after she and her family sustained “minor” injuries in a car crash, her campaign announced on Sunday.
articles.body: Former Rep. Mary Peltola is rescheduling several upcoming campaign events after she and her family sustained “minor” injuries in a car crash, her campaign announced on Sunday. “Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits. Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary’s upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover,” Peltola campaign manager Cheryl Bruce said in a statement. “Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always Tour, and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail to speak directly with Alaskans about her plan to take on the rigged system and lower costs for working families,” Bruce added. Peltola was en route to the Alaska Federation of Natives’ annual banquet on Saturday when a vehicle transporting the candidate and her family was struck by another driver, according to the campaign. The police department in Anchorage confirmed Sunday that a collision involving three vehicles occurred on Saturday evening and those involved sustained “non-life threatening injuries.” Police added that the incident is under investigation. Peltola, a Democrat, is locked in a competitive Senate race against GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan. She was elected to the House in 2022 but narrowly lost her re-election bid in 2024, the same year that President Donald Trump won the state by 13 percentage points. Sullivan’s re-election race, in which he’s seeking a third term, is tighter than expected, with Alaska voters tying Trump to high gas and grocery prices resulting from the ongoing war with Iran. Trump and Vice President JD Vance rallied voters in Alaska separately earlier this month. Republicans have accused Democrats of recruiting another candidate named Dan Sullivan to run for the Senate, saying that voters may be confused by the presence of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot if they plan to vote for the incumbent senator. Democrats have not taken credit for recruiting the second Dan Sullivan into the race. He’ll appear on the ballot as Dan J. Sullivan, while the incumbent senator will be identified by his name, political party and a clear notation that he’s the incumbent. Last week, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit against Alaska’s election officials, seeking to block certification of the election if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. They cited Dan J. Sullivan’s presence on the ballot as a point of “voter confusion.” On Saturday, Democrats filed a motion urging a federal judge to dismiss the case.

articles.title: This week on the Hill: Trump, Obama lead final push before Election Day
articles.summary: It’s the final full week before Election Day, and candidates are ramping up their campaigns with rallies, high-profile surrogates and a last round of debates. After a week of daily campaign events across the United States, President Trump is set to visit Corinth, Miss., on Monday, in support of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (Miss.). He…
articles.body:
It’s the final full week before Election Day, and candidates are ramping up their campaigns with rallies, high-profile surrogates and a last round of debates.

After a week of daily campaign events across the United States, President Trump is set to visit Corinth, Miss., on Monday, in support of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (Miss.). He will also be holding two rallies Tuesday in Texas, where he is expected to campaign for candidates including Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R). On Wednesday, the president will travel to Chillicothe, Ohio.

Former President Obama is also hitting the campaign trail, headlining a “United for Georgia” rally in Atlanta on Wednesday to support Sen. Jon Ossoff’s (D-Ga.) reelection bid and urge voters to turn out on Election Day. He held two rallies Saturday, one in Ohio and the other in Michigan.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris is slated to join the push as well. The NAACP announced that Harris will partner with the group’s president and CEO, Derrick Johnson, for civic engagement events in Milwaukee and Atlanta.

The final stretch will also feature a slate of debates.

In Pennsylvania, Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R-Pa.) and Democratic challenger Paige Cognetti are expected to face off Thursday in a debate hosted by WVIA News. In New Hampshire, Republican John Sununu and Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) are scheduled to debate Wednesday in an event hosted by WMUR-TV.

Trump to stump for GOP candidates: The president is making a last-minute effort to boost Republican momentum as voter frustration over the economy and the Iran war take over this election cycle.

Obama to hit up rally in Georgia: The former president will headline the event with Ossoff and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms on Wednesday.

Harris to encourage voters to turn out: Harris’s role in the 2026 midterms comes as there’s speculation she will launch a 2028 presidential bid.

Challengers to face off in final debates: Bresnahan and Cognetti are running to represent Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District, while Pappas and Sununu are vying for the open New Hampshire Senate seat.

GOP anxiety on full display as Trump barnstorms

Trump’s appearances across Mississippi, Texas and Ohio come as Republicans have been neck and neck, or in some cases, trailing their Democratic opponents in key races.

Democratic candidate James Talarico, for instance, is in a dead heat with Paxton for the Senate in Texas, according to a recent survey from Emerson College Polling and The Hill. The survey found that 48 percent of respondents would back Talarico, while 46 percent said they would back Paxton, a result within the poll’s margin of error. Another 5 percent of respondents were undecided, and 1 percent picked Libertarian Ted Brown.

“Since August, Talarico’s support has slowly inched up by about a point each month, from 46% to 48%, while Paxton has hovered between 46% and 47%,” Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling, said.

In Ohio, Sen. Jon Husted (R) is locked in a toss-up race against former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) to hold onto his Senate seat, while Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat Amy Acton are locked in a similarly tight race for the governor’s mansion. Democrats have signaled they are feeling increasingly optimistic about both races.

Ramaswamy, in particular, has come under scrutiny after he confirmed to reporters last week his campaign was behind an attack ad featuring Acton’s estranged, biological mother Donna Arthur, who insinuated her daughter has mental health issues.

Several Republicans quickly denounced Ramaswamy’s ad, and the nonpartisan Cook Political Report shifted the Ohio governor’s race from “toss-up” to “lean Democrat.”

And in Mississippi, Hyde-Smith is facing an unexpectedly tough contest against Democrat Scott Colom. The seat is rated as likely Republican by the Cook Political Report, but Democrats are still hoping to flip it as their momentum grows in the midterms.

Obama campaigns for Ossoff, Bottoms in Georgia

The former president isn’t done with politics.

Obama will be making his way to Atlanta, where he is expected to stump for Ossoff and Bottoms on Wednesday. The Cook Political Report rates the Georgia governor’s race as a “toss-up” and the Senate race as “likely” Democratic.

A poll from The Atlanta Journal-Constitution and the University of Georgia reported that 48 percent of respondents supported Ossoff’s reelection bid, 40 percent backed his Republican opponent, Rep. Mike Collins, and 12 percent were undecided.

Ossoff, the only Senate Democrat running for reelection in a state Trump handily won in 2024, is running for his second term following a high-profile 2020 runoff election. He faced off against Collins earlier this month in a debate; they clashed on the Jeffrey Epstein files, Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran.

In the gubernatorial race, 46 percent of poll respondents backed Republican Rick Jackson, 45 percent supported Bottoms and 8 percent remained undecided. Jackson’s lead is within the poll’s margin of error, meaning the candidates are essentially deadlocked.

Harris to headline civic engagement events with the NAACP

Harris is slated to join NAACP’s Johnson to headline several events aimed at driving up turnout in the 2026 midterms, including one in Wisconsin on Monday and another in Atlanta on Thursday.

“The NAACP has been at the forefront of protecting voting rights and ensuring our communities have a voice in our democracy,” Johnson said in a press release . “Our work doesn’t begin or end on Election Day. From voter education to grassroots organizing, we remain committed to building informed, engaged communities. We look forward to continuing that work alongside Vice President Harris in Milwaukee and Atlanta.”

Harris’s appearances come as she has said she “might” run for president in 2028. Many see her as a top contender to serve as Democrats’ nominee, recent polls suggest.

Harris has also embarked on a campaign blitz in October before Election Day with other stops in Mississippi and New Hampshire, according to her office.

Republicans and Democrats face off in House and Senate debates

Sununu and Pappas are expected to debate Wednesday.

A recent New Hampshire Institute of Politics survey, commissioned by AARP, found the Democrat holds a 7-point advantage over his Republican opponent among likely voters in the state.

The candidates are competing in the November race for the open seat to replace retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.).

Sununu served in both chambers of Congress for more than a decade before he lost his Senate seat to Shaheen in 2008. His father is John H. Sununu, and his brother is Chris Sununu — both of whom served as governors of New Hampshire.

Pappas has represented the Granite State in the House since 2019, and he has been part of the Problem Solvers Caucus since 2023.

The state has not elected a Republican senator in more than a decade, although the GOP has controlled the state’s governor’s mansion since 2017.

Meanwhile in Pennsylvania, Bresnahan and Cognetti are expected to spar Thursday. The Cook Political Report has rated Bresnahan’s seat as a toss-up.

Cognetti, who has served as the mayor of Scranton, Pa., since 2020, engaged in a candidate forum last week with Bresnahan, where the two discussed childcare, boosting small businesses, immigration and other pressing issues.

Julia Mueller, Julia Manchester, Sarah Davis and Mira Bhakta contributed to this report.

articles.title: Catholic bishops regret White House prayer photo with Trump, say it was used politically
articles.summary: Two Catholic bishops have expressed regret about agreeing to a White House meeting that produced a publicly distributed photo of them praying with President...
articles.body:
Two Catholic bishops have expressed regret about agreeing to a White House meeting that produced a publicly distributed photo of them praying with President Donald Trump.

Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, in a statement titled "A Public Apology," said Sunday that he had received many questions and comments — some of them distraught — about the meeting on Thursday which he and 11 other bishops attended.

He said the meeting was speedily publicized by the White House with photos and a video, without consent of the participants, and less than two weeks away from the midterm elections .

"I feel a heavy sadness, not only over the pain I caused, but also for the fact that something so sacred to a group of religious leaders, prayer to our Heavenly Father, would be manipulated in that way," Grob said.

The bishop of Des Moines, Iowa, William Joensen, also issued a statement making clear he felt the White House had taken advantage of the bishops.

"I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purpose," he wrote. "I pray I am more prudent and wise going forward, even as I remain resolute in my openness to engaging and praying for political leaders at all levels."

Asked whether the White House had or hadn't received the bishop's consent for releasing the photos and video, the press office declined to answer that question. Instead, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers replied, "There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it."

The White House invitation to the bishops — extended in September — offered discussion about such issues as immigration enforcement, religious worker visas , abortion and use of federal tax credits to support private education, according to Joensen and Grob.

"The meeting was in no way an endorsement of the president, his policies, or his party," wrote Grob. "We were told the meeting was to be a private discussion, that several Catholic members of the cabinet might make an appearance, and that there could be an opportunity to pray privately with the president."

"It did not take long thereafter for the White House to post a video and photos of the prayer," Grob said.

"I soon began receiving messages of serious concern over the possibility that I had inadvertently participated in a political event less than two weeks before a national election," he added. "I also heard from some who felt wounded because of the ways they or their family had been harmed by the president's policies."

"I did not go without reservations. I wish I had heeded them," Grob concluded. "I apologize for any damage my actions have done."

Collectively, members of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops have diverse views on Trump and his administration's policies. Minnesota-based Bishop Robert Barron, for example, agreed to serve on Trump's Religious Liberty Commission, which was filled almost entirely with conservative Christians. Some other bishops vehemently denounced aspects of Trump's tough stance on immigration enforcement , saying it runs counter to Catholic teaching.

articles.title: Aleksandar Vucic: Serbia's veteran ruler felled by student-led movement
articles.summary: The dominant force in Serbian politics for over 14 years, Aleksandar Vucic, who conceded defeat in a snap parliamentary poll on Sunday, rose from the wreckag...
articles.body:
The dominant force in Serbian politics for over 14 years, Aleksandar Vucic, who conceded defeat in a snap parliamentary poll on Sunday, rose from the wreckage of strongman Slobodan Milosevic's cabinet to the centre of power using his brand of populist nationalism.

For supporters, the 56-year-old represented stability, development and patriotism in a country scarred by the bloody wars of the 1990s and ensuing international isolation.

But opponents saw him as an increasingly authoritarian figure, twisting between the Kremlin and Brussels and leading a government accused of endemic corruption.

Vucic conceded his party had lost after voters cast ballots in record numbers in Sunday's vote, defeated by a new political force that emerged from a years-long protest movement.

"Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we lost these elections," Vucic told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade.

Vucic rose to prominence in the 1990s as an ultra-nationalist ally of Milosevic, serving as his information minister in 1998.

After protests ousted the Yugoslav strongman in 2000, Vucic became a senior figure in the far-right Serbian Radical Party.

He was then a vocal supporter of Bosnian Serb political and military leaders Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, both later sentenced to life for genocide and other crimes committed during the Bosnian war.

But Vucic underwent a dramatic rebrand in 2008, co-founding the conservative, pro-European Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which won parliamentary elections in 2012 and has dominated Serbian politics since.

He served as deputy prime minister, defence minister and prime minister before becoming president in 2017.

Even after polishing his image, Vucic has been reluctant to distance himself from nationalist leanings and far-right associates.

He has stopped short of condemning Serbs convicted of atrocities during the 1990s conflicts and looked the other way as pro-government media and political allies openly praised war criminals.

Despite trying to deny state involvement in a large funeral gathering for Mladic in the Serbian capital last month, several of his ministers attended, drawing sharp criticism from Brussels.

A relentless campaigner, he maintained a near-constant presence on pro-government television channels, embracing locals in tiny rural villages and chastising critics during lengthy news conferences.

He has cultivated the image of a tireless leader criss-crossing Serbia, attracting investment and creating jobs.

At the same time, he has juggled the competing interests of European Union aspirations and Serbia's close ties to Russia.

Supporters praised him as a brave defender of Serbian sovereignty, spending billions of euros on defence -- as he warned of foreign influence and pressure from NATO-member neighbours.

He often cited Serbia's infrastructure and improved living standards as proof of his success, once pledging to make the country a "land of cranes".

From the gleaming waterfront district to the numerous projects unfolding in preparation for Expo 2027, his party's slogan "United Serbia" is plastered on billboards across the capital.

But when a concrete canopy collapsed at a newly renovated train station in 2024 killing 16 people, the accusations of corruption which had dogged many of his signature projects caused an outpouring of anger.

Student-led demonstrations calling for transparent investigations drew hundreds of thousands to the streets in the largest protests since the Milosevic era.

As demands grew into calls for snap elections, Vucic and his supporters pushed back.

Students manning university blockades were labelled tools of foreign powers.

In September, nearly two years into the protests, Vucic finally called snap elections for October, citing "major turbulence on the domestic political scene", thus meeting a key student demand.

"All of this will end on October 25," Vucic said, referring to the protests, at a major pre-election rally in Novi Sad, the city where the canopy had collapsed.
