articles.title: Hinson calls Putin ‘murderer,’ says US should not make deals with Russia
articles.summary: Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) on Sunday called Russian President Vladimir Putin a “murderer” and urged that the U.S. not make any deals with Russia. ABC News’s “This Week” host Jonathan Karl asked Hinson, a Senate candidate and a staunch supporter of Ukraine, what she made of U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff’s remark to Putin last…
articles.body:
Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) on Sunday called Russian President Vladimir Putin a “murderer” and urged that the U.S. not make any deals with Russia.

ABC News’s “This Week” host Jonathan Karl asked Hinson , a Senate candidate and a staunch supporter of Ukraine, what she made of U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff’s remark to Putin last week calling the Russian leader a “ humanitarian .”

“He’s not a humanitarian, he is a murderer,” she said. “I don’t think we should be making deals with murderers and dictators, and that’s why I stood up for Ukraine. I think that Ukraine is a freedom-loving country … We should not be allowing a dictator to win.”

Hinson said she traveled to Ukraine to meet with its president, Volodymyr Zelensky, and called the country’s people “incredibly resilient.” She reiterated that the U.S. should not make deals with Russia, saying she voted for a sanctions package targeting Russia. President Trump waived sanctions on Russia weeks later.

“And, frankly, I’ve been banned from going [to Russia], so I think that sends a very clear message about my approach to Russia,” Hinson continued. “Again, I want to bring all these conflicts abroad to an end as quickly as possible. I don’t think anybody likes forever wars, but certainly we cannot be empowering dictators to win more.”

Karl said the Iowa Republican outlined two strong differences between her and Trump, and asked how she would challenge him on those fronts.

“You challenge him in person, right?” she said. “And that’s exactly what I’ve done. I’m not afraid to tell him when I think he’s wrong on something. And again, when he’s right, I will be the fiercest ally for someone. And I think that’s how Iowans expect you to do your job. They don’t like empty rhetoric.”

Witkoff faced backlash for the praise he gave Putin during a meeting in St. Petersburg, Russia, where the special envoy announced the release of American teacher Stephen Hubbard. Republican lawmakers questioned the remark, with Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) writing on the social platform X , “WTF, Steve?”

Trump’s executive order earlier this month to waive sanctions on Russia was also met with blowback from lawmakers . He said last Wednesday that Hubbard’s release was related to waiving sanctions meant to strangle Russia’s ability to continue waging its war on Ukraine, and he received “numerous” apologies after criticizing him.

“If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt,” he wrote on Truth Social.

The response to the waiver was coupled with Trump’s diesel deal with the Kremlin, with the intent to lower diesel prices amid the energy shortage caused by the Iran war. Lawmakers slammed the deal , with five House Republicans signing a letter urging that he cancel the deal.

articles.title: US Attorney General Todd Blanche defends Alaska Senate election lawsuit
articles.summary: The Department of Justice has faced criticism that its lawsuit is aimed at blocking a Democratic victory in a key race.
articles.body:
United States Attorney General Todd Blanche has defended the Department of Justice’s decision to sue to prevent the certification of a Republican loss in Alaska’s tight Senate race.

On Sunday, Blanche did a tour of the morning political shows in the US, making stops at CNN’s State of the Union TV programme and CBS’s Face the Nation.

In each appearance, he faced pointed questions about the legality of the Justice Department’s efforts, responding, in some cases, with open frustration.

“ Why is this controversial?” Blanche asked CNN host Dana Bash at one point. He proceeded to accuse one of the candidates in the Senate race of intentionally trying to confuse voters.

“We’re going to try to create a situation where that can be remedied,” he said. “That shouldn’t be something that is causing this shock and horror.”

But the Justice Department’s lawsuit , filed on October 22, has been the subject of bipartisan criticism.

Many have accused the administration of President Donald Trump of laying the groundwork to block a Democratic win in the race. Trump himself claimed to have authorised the lawsuit.

“I’m the one who said do it,” he told reporters on Friday.

During the midterm elections on November 3, citizens in Alaska will vote in one of the closest Senate races in the country, which will help decide whether Republicans maintain their majority in the chamber.

Senator Dan S Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, is seeking to defend his seat in the US Senate. But he faces fierce competition from former US Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat.

Also in the running is another candidate named Dan J Sullivan, a former Forest Service employee.

The second Sullivan’s decision to run has raised concerns that he is a spoiler candidate, whose presence on the ballot is designed to draw votes away from the incumbent.

But the Forest Service worker has denied any such intent. Such allegations, he said, are “entirely false”.

“I am not a registered Democrat, and I have had no conversations whatsoever with the Peltola campaign about my candidacy,” the second Sullivan wrote in a letter to Alaska’s lieutenant governor before the state’s primaries.

“I have considered running for political office for over a decade. I made the decision to formally run for the United States Senate in the upcoming primary election because Senator Sullivan has routinely failed the people of Alaska, and they deserve a better representative. It is my right to do so.”

Four candidates advanced to the final round of voting after Alaska’s August primaries. They included Peltola and both Sullivans. The two men are running as Republicans.

The Justice Department has argued that its lawsuit – filed less than two weeks before the midterm elections – is necessary “to protect the integrity” of the election.

Any result in the Senate race, it argues, would be “tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J Sullivan”.

The department has therefore called on the US District Court in Alaska to issue an order declaring the race’s certification “unlawful” and barring the state from “allowing such a certification to occur”.

Under the US Constitution, only states have the power to administer elections, though Congress has the right to pass regulations concerning federal votes.

It is highly unusual for a presidential administration to inject itself into issues of state election certification, and experts say such a move is likely to be deemed illegal.

Already, in June, Alaska’s Supreme Court ruled that both Sullivans could compete in the Senate race. The state’s Division of Elections has also taken steps to reduce voter confusion.

The November 3 ballot, for instance, will list Dan S Sullivan as the incumbent and as a “registered Republican”.

Dan J Sullivan, meanwhile, will have the suffix “Jr” added to his name, and his party affiliation will be left blank, despite the candidate identifying as Republican.

But in Sunday’s television appearances, Blanche — who leads the Department of Justice and formerly served as Trump’s personal lawyer — argued that merely having two Sullivans on the ballot is a recipe for confusion.

“It is wrong,” Blanche told CNN. “Putting aside whether we’re going to win or lose in the courts, putting aside what the Alaskan Supreme Court has done, in our system, we should not have a candidate who has to worry about another candidate being on the ballot for no other reason than to confuse voters.”

Blanche also denied any impropriety in Trump saying he ordered the lawsuit.

“He’s supposed to make sure that everything in this country is running right, including elections,” Blanche said.

Historically, the Justice Department has embraced a norm of judicial independence, though critics have accused the Trump administration of wielding its prosecutorial powers for political gain.

Bash, the CNN host, raised some of those concerns, pointing to Trump’s comments accusing Democrats of cheating, as well as his history of election denialism.

The president has long denied his loss in the 2020 presidential race, and his supporters sought to block the certification of that election, notably by storming the US Capitol on January 6, 2021.

When Bash pointed to that incident, Blanche chided her: “Oh, you’ve got to stop it with that.”

“Why are you yelling at me?” Bash responded as the two talked over each other.

“You are not being a real person. Come on, man,” Blanche continued. “That is crazy.”

He also denied that Trump was setting the stage for a contested election if the Democrat Peltola were to win. Instead, he framed the lawsuit as setting the stage for further investigations into any eventual results.

“The relief that we’re seeking – which, again, isn’t to determine who the senator is, it’s not to try to overturn something the state is going to do – it’s just to make sure that the ballots that come in are kept in a way that may allow a court to investigate further,” Blanche said.

Speaking to CBS, Blanche also dodged a question about whether Trump personally asked him to file the lawsuit.

“I will never, ever, ever talk about communications that I have with the president of the United States. I never have, and I never will,” Blanche said.

The race to control the US Senate is expected to be a nail-biter, with Republicans holding a slim majority at present: They have 53 seats in the 100-member chamber.

Only a third of the Senate’s seats – 35 in total – will be up for grabs in the midterm races, as terms in the chamber last six years and are staggered across different election years.

Trump’s Republican Party is projected to face an uphill battle to protect its congressional majorities, amid backlash against the rising cost of living and Trump’s own withering poll numbers.

Roughly seven Senate elections are considered toss-ups, including the Alaska race.

In early October, The New York Times and Siena College released a poll finding Peltola leading the incumbent Sullivan by nearly 7 percentage points, one of the widest margins of any of the toss-up states.

articles.title: Rogers dodges questions on MAGA label, Trump tariffs
articles.summary: Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) dodged questions on whether he identifies as a MAGA-Republican and avoided clarifying his position on President Trump’s controversial tariffs against Canada ahead of his competitive race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate race. During a Sunday appearance on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Rogers was asked if he considered himself…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) dodged questions on whether he identifies as a MAGA-Republican and avoided clarifying his position on President Trump’s controversial tariffs against Canada ahead of his competitive race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate race.

During a Sunday appearance on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Rogers was asked if he considered himself a MAGA Republican.

“Listen, I’m going to tell you this is, I get you guys on the national press, but this is a little bit disgusting to me,” Rogers told host Kristen Welker, adding that a former Michigan Democratic Party chair declined to back El-Sayed’s bid.

The former lawmaker was asked again if he identified with the label.

“Let me-I’m going to go right back through this. There is a reason we have support from people in Detroit and Flint and Pontiac, because we’re there talking about issues, talking about their needs and future, and [El-Sayed] is too extreme for them,” Rogers stated. “Nobody wants to talk about it in the national press. We invite you to come to Michigan, talk to some of these people.”

Earlier in the interview, Welker asked Rogers about a past comment he made calling for an end to the ongoing trade war with Canada, saying, “If you were elected, would you vote to repeal some of President Trump’s tariffs?”

“Well, again, the best way to do this is walk in and say, ‘Can we work this out?’ And I’ll give you a great example of how I’ve done that,” Rogers said, detailing his push to stop Canadian garbage trucks from dumping trash in the U.S.

“But if you’re going to tariff anything, tariff this trash that’s filling up our landfills from what is the third largest landmass country in the world,” he continued. “You know the automobile portion of these Canadian tariffs worries me a little bit, and we’re going to go back and work through those issues to get some relief to make sure that it’s good for Michigan, not bad for Michigan. There are other tariffs.”

Several polls from September show El-Sayed with a narrow lead over Rogers.

Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s partner, forecasts that the Democrat has a 67 percent chance of winning the seat left open by retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.).

Trump headed to Michigan on Sunday in an effort to boost Rogers’s chances though it is unclear if that will help close the gap between the candidates.

articles.title: Appeals court resists DOJ’s bid to immediately segregate 20k California ballots
articles.summary: A federal appeals court appeared unlikely to immediately agree to the Trump administration’s bid to segregate 20,000 California ballots it says are likely noncitizen voters, expressing skepticism at a rare Sunday hearing that a trial judge needs to move quicker. “I don’t see how we have jurisdiction,” said U.S. Circuit Judge Mark Bennett. The Justice Department (DOJ) sued…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court appeared unlikely to immediately agree to the Trump administration’s bid to segregate 20,000 California ballots it says are likely noncitizen voters, expressing skepticism at a rare Sunday hearing that a trial judge needs to move quicker.

“I don’t see how we have jurisdiction,” said U.S. Circuit Judge Mark Bennett.

The Justice Department (DOJ) sued California earlier this month as the state rebuffed claims that it sent ballots to 20,000 likely noncitizens as part of its universal mail voting program. The DOJ wants the ballots segregated and verified before they can be counted. It’s one of multiple lawsuits the administration has launched in recent weeks as the midterm elections quickly approach.

A trial judge is set to hold a hearing on Tuesday, but the DOJ says action is needed sooner, because ballots are already being submitted. Los Angeles County alone has already processed 331,000 mail ballots, court filings show.

The DOJ declined to wait and has headed straight to a three-judge panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9 th Circuit. It agreed to convene on the weekend, but once underway, the administration faced an icy reception, particularly from Bennett and U.S. Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez.

“It gave you the essentially the timing you wanted for a hearing,” Bennett said.

Beyond timing, both Bennett and Sanchez raised concerns about the reliability of the administration’s list and whether it actually reflects the one California used to send out mail ballots this election cycle.

“You were not able to explain who these third parties are that form some part in the chain of analysis over this list,” Sanchez pushed back. “And the reliability of the list — very much — your claims very much depend on the reliability of that list.”

DOJ attorney Matthew Donnelly indicated the list was purchased from the state and supplied to the administration. To assuage any concerns, he pointed the judges to sworn declarations from Department of Homeland Security officials.

Bennett was appointed by President Trump and Sanchez was appointed by former President Biden.

The third judge on the panel, Patrick Bumatay, another Trump appointee, appeared the most sympathetic to the administration.

Even as he warned on Sunday that a court intervention may lead to confusion among local officials, at turns, he pushed back on the notion that the administration’s arguments would unconstitutionally commandeer them to enforce federal regulations.

“It’s not extraordinary to ask California to verify citizenship of a voter,” Bumatay said.

“It is in the manner that the federal government is asking for here,” responded Sam Siegel, representing the state.

articles.title: Tillis accuses California of being ‘guilty’ of ballot harvesting: ‘They have a system there that is ripe for abuse’
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) on Sunday accused the state of California of being “guilty” of ballot harvesting, claiming that the Golden State has “a system there that is ripe for abuse.” “Face the Nation” host Margaret Brennan asked about the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) legal battle with the state over potential noncitizens on their voter…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) on Sunday accused the state of California of being “guilty” of ballot harvesting , claiming that the Golden State has “a system there that is ripe for abuse.”

“Face the Nation” host Margaret Brennan asked about the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) legal battle with the state over potential noncitizens on their voter rolls, and the threat of legal consequences if mail-in ballots continue to be sent out.

Along with the DOJ’s preemptive lawsuit against Alaska to block certifying its votes if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses in November and the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), Brennan asked if there was a pattern and if Tillis was “comfortable with these actions this close to an election.”

“Well, I think we have to be careful,” Tillis said. “First, you’ve got to take them separately. California has been guilty of ballot harvesting. They have a policy to do it. They have a system there that is ripe for abuse and they need to be looked at.”

The DOJ sued the state earlier this month after giving California officials 48 hours to set aside the ballots of the 20,000 noncitizens to be given to the Department of Homeland Security. The department previously warned that California officials could face legal action if they did not comply, with President Trump claiming they “will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!”

The department reportedly sent letters to every county in the state asking that they identify potential noncitizens on their voter rolls, a task that top federal prosecutor in Southern California, Bill Essayli, called “simple.”

The DOJ’s letters included a list of people federal officials claimed the agency has identified as possible noncitizens who may receive ballots through California’s practice of sending a ballot to every registered voter in the state.

“California does not verify citizenship status. We did the work for them,” Essayli wrote on social media. “We obtained the registered voter list and told them who we believe are noncitizens on their rolls. Knowingly processing noncitizen ballots is a federal crime under 18 U.S.C. §§ 611 and 2. We will hold election officials accountable. No one is above the law.”

Last Thursday, the DOJ requested that the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals intervene by temporarily blocking the state from counting the ballots. This came days after 28 people accused of not being U.S. citizens were charged in connection with illegally registered votes. These 28 people were alleged by the DOJ to be among the 20,000 noncitizens.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) has fired back at the DOJ and Trump, last week accusing the president of “trying to quite literally rig the election.”

“He’s trying to get our voter rolls,” he said at a campaign rally. “You can’t make this stuff up.”

articles.title: Trump says El-Sayed should have to pass through metal detector to enter Senate
articles.summary: President Trump called out Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, saying he should have to pass through a metal detector to enter the Senate building. “Anyone with that record of support for jihadists would be screened and unable to get a seat on an airplane. They certainly should not give him a seat in…
articles.body:
President Trump called out Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, saying he should have to pass through a metal detector to enter the Senate building.

“Anyone with that record of support for jihadists would be screened and unable to get a seat on an airplane. They certainly should not give him a seat in the United States Senate,” Trump said while rallying in Michigan .

“He would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate. I want him to have a metal detector,” the president continued.

El-Sayed would be the first Muslim senator if he wins Michigan’s open Senate race against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.). The Michigan Democrat has faced numerous attacks on the campaign trail about his family background and faith, including past comments made by his mother and half-sister.

In a Truth Social post before his rally in Michigan, Trump referred to El-Sayed as “a Jihadist Member of the Muslim Brotherhood,” adding that he believed the Senate candidate wanted “our Country to go to Sharia Law.”

During the latest candidate debate between the pair, Rogers similarly pointed out political contributions made to El-Sayed from people connected to the Muslim Brotherhood, claiming the Democrat “ pledged his support ” to the organization.

El-Sayed has disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood and his campaign has repeatedly denied that he has any connection to the group, which President Trump designated as a terrorist group last year.

A Marist poll found El-Sayed narrowly leading Rogers by 2 points, though this lead is within the poll’s margin of error meaning both candidates are dead locked.

Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, predicted the battleground Senate election leaning in favor of El-Sayed, forecasting him with a 67 percent chance of winning. While Cook Political Report rated the race as a “toss up” with both parties equal on its partisan voting index.

El-Sayed’s campaign did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: The future of the GOP in New England rides on Maine’s Senate vote
articles.summary: Susan Collins faces Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine's Senate race as New England's last Republican senator fights to prove centrism still works.
articles.body: The New England region of the United States comprises six states, more than 15 million people, 21 seats in the House of Representatives, and 12 senators. Yet, of this congressional delegation, only one is a Republican — Sen. Susan Collins of Maine — at least for now. In the Pine Tree State, Democrat Troy Jackson has a slight lead in the polls. Over her 30 years in the Senate, Collins has pulled a lot of electoral footballs from Democrat Charlie Browns, who thought victory and a Senate seat were a chip shot away. In Maine, I chatted with Republican State House Representative Laurel Libby — a rising star in the local GOP and possible heir to the kind of centrist Republicanism that Collins has managed to cling to in this mostly blue region. Libby told Fox News Digital that "[Collins] is great on constituent services and goes out of her way to be in the community," adding, "it's kind of hysterical for Troy Jackson to say she doesn’t hold town halls. Susan Collins is out in the community constantly." DAVID MARCUS: IN BLUE MAINE, NOBODY BELIEVES SUSAN COLLINS WILL LOSE UNTIL THEY SEE IT I pressed Libby a bit on what role, especially if Collins holds on to win, the Maine and broader New England Republican Party can play in the post Trump era — which lies just over two years over the horizon. She replied, "I think we need to be providing the long-term solutions for Maine. "We’ve seen what a Democrat trifecta [in state government] has done for Maine. During Jackson’s time in the Senate, he is responsible for our electricity costs going up 70%," she said. "He supported a budget that went up 50%." VOTERS PREPARE TO WEIGH-IN ON TRUMP'S ECONOMY AS COSTS CONTINUE TO SURGE These were concerns that I also heard from Don, a Vietnam veteran in his late 70s who recently moved into Bangor from a nearby farm after his wife passed away. "All those Democrats south of [the state capital] Augusta, they just think everyone is made of money, and it's really hurting normal folks," Don said. Among Republican voters in Bangor, and even some Independents, the word "Augusta," is generally uttered with approximately the level of disdain Jerry Seinfeld had when saying "Newman!" Dan and Tess, a couple in their 30s, were in town from Massachusetts, of which Maine was once a part. They both see Collins as a strong centrist voice for the region. "It's a problem when every politician in New England is a Democrat," Dan said. "Especially when the Democrats are out of power." Chris, also from Massachusetts, was in Maine upgrading carrier lines. When asked what Republicans could do to get a foothold in the region, he said, "I don't really know, when the state's been Democratic [for so long]. ... Coming together to the people with things that don't pull sides apart, because they have two sides, but they're supposed to meet in the middle." This is a point that Libby refined in our conversation when asked about the fact that Collins was campaigning this week with former moderate Democratic Senator Joe Manchin of West Virginia, while Jackson barnstormed with far-left New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. KYRSTEN SINEMA QUESTIONS WHETHER MODERATES STILL HAVE A PLACE IN THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY "It’s absolutely representative of what they both [would] bring to the Senate," Libby told Fox News Digital. "Susan Collins has proven that she is willing and able to work in a bipartisan manner, to get things done, and during his time in the [state] Senate, did the opposite," including Libby claims a few end runs around the Maine Constitution. Manchin is now out of power, mostly owing to his refusal to bow to the far left zeitgeist of the current Democratic Party. This is thus far a fate Susan Collins has avoided over the past decade when she distances herself from Trump and MAGA populism. If Troy Jackson does manage to topple Collins, the message to Republicans in Maine and New England will be that centrism doesn’t work, that they need bare knuckle brawlers more like Rep. Brandon Gill of Texas, than bipartisan peacemakers like Collins. Nationally, there are some hardcore Republicans who would welcome a Collins loss in this respect. They see moderate Republicans as more of an obstacle than an asset. But most in the GOP concede that holding the Senate for Trump’s final two years in office outweighs the broader ideological intraparty fights. Win, lose, or draw for Collins, in the future it will be younger Republican politicians like Libby, who will have to define what a Republican is in Maine, New England, and to some degree in America as a whole. Democrats exiled Joe Manchin for his lack of political purity; they are on the way to doing the same to Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., even though, somewhat hilariously, he really could wind up as the 51st vote in a one-seat Democratic majority next year. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP If Maine Republicans can save Susan Collins once again, it will show that the GOP really can, at least in part, and unlike Democrats, embrace moderate and centrist positions — a point that could play heavily in their favor as both parties try to define themselves for the post-Trump age.

articles.title: Trump leans into Islamophobic rhetoric at Michigan rally
articles.summary: The president attacked Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee who is locked in a dead heat against Republican Mike Rogers.
articles.body: President Donald Trump embraced Islamophobic rhetoric Sunday as he rallied in Port Huron, Michigan, in support of the state’s Republican candidates, including the GOP Senate nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers. Trump alleged that Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee who is locked in a dead heat with Rogers, is a “jihadist,” calling him a “Muslim Brotherhood member” while saying Rogers is “apple pie.” “Anyone with that record of support for jihadists would be screened and unable to get a seat on an airplane. They certainly should not give him a seat in the United States Senate,” Trump said about El-Sayed. “He would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate. I want him to have a metal detector.” Trump went on to draw a comparison between the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks and El-Sayed as he introduced speaker David Beamer, whose son, Todd Beamer, was a passenger who died on the hijacked United Flight 93. “Twenty-five years later, Michigan needs to stand up and fight just like Todd did to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol,” Trump said. Beamer went on to extend Trump’s comparison between the Senate race and 9/11. “What has changed? Well, one thing is 9/11 was a surprise attack. What’s going on right now in our country and here in Michigan? It’s not a surprise. We can see the attack coming that culminates in this battleground state on Tuesday, November the 3rd,” Beamer said as Trump stood behind him onstage. “What’s different this time is the enemy has not come from abroad. The enemy is right here among us, local terrorists, local citizens that want to demolish our country,” he added. Beamer, who has been featured in Rogers’ campaign ads, compared the two men and claimed Rogers is “an American” while saying El-Sayed is not, going on to call him “anti-American.” “Abdul has a birth certificate. The birth certificate says he’s a citizen of America. You know what? A birth certificate doesn’t make you an American,” Beamer said. “He has blood that’s red. However, he has chosen to remove any strain of the white and blue part in his life. We cannot, cannot allow this man to invade and occupy our country,” he added. Both Rogers and El-Sayed were born in Michigan. El-Sayed’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump’s and Beamer’s remarks. Trump has accused El-Sayed of having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, an international Sunni Islamist organization founded in Egypt in 1928. The Trump administration has designated certain chapters of the group in Lebanon, Jordan and Egypt as terrorist organizations. El-Sayed has repeatedly denied any ties to the group, which he has denounced. El-Sayed went viral for a heated interaction last week with a town hall attendee who asked him to condemn the organization. “You assume ... that because I am Muslim, that somehow I would have some allegiance to something that is not our Constitution,” El-Sayed told the attendee last week. Rogers was asked Sunday about Trump’s calling El-Sayed a “Muslim Brotherhood jihadist” and a “violent terrorist” in an interview on NBC’s “Meet the Press.” Pressed about whether he agreed with Trump’s characterizations, Rogers said the election is about “me versus Abdul,” adding, “I’ve never called him a terrorist.” Rogers has previously questioned El-Sayed about his mother, Fatten Elkomy, over her work decades ago at a charity the U.S. government later labeled a supporter of terrorist groups, leading to its closure. Elkomy was not accused of wrongdoing at the time. Trump helped popularize a false conspiracy theory about former President Barack Obama, claiming he was not a U.S. citizen and demanding to see his birth certificate. He has since repurposed “birther” attacks against other political rivals, including former U.N. Ambassador Nikki Haley, who was born in South Carolina. Trump on Sunday referred to Obama, who rallied in Detroit on Saturday on behalf of El-Sayed and other Michigan Democratic candidates. “My competitor was here yesterday,” Trump, who is not running for office, said about Obama, who is also not running for office. “He didn’t have a crowd like this, I can tell you.”

articles.title: Nicki Minaj joins Trump onstage at Michigan rally
articles.summary: The Super Bass singer is the latest big name to campaign in Michigan, where a tight Senate race is playing out ahead of the 3 November midterms.
articles.body:
Rapper Nicki Minaj said US President Donald Trump has "changed the energy of the country" as she joined him at a Michigan rally to stump for Republicans ahead of the nationwide midterm elections.

"He's given us a future to look forward to," she said, after Trump praised her figure and called her on stage to speak.

Minaj has called herself Trump's "number one fan" despite criticising some of his policies in his first term.

In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is locked in a tight race with Republican Mike Rogers with just over a week to go before the midterms. Former President Barack Obama held a rally - one of the first in this cycle - with the Democrat on Saturday.

Democrats are also aggressively hitting the campaign trail, with close elections taking place on 3 November which will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency.

In his remarks on Sunday, Trump focused on El-Sayed's Muslim faith and background, alleging that he will "invite jihadists" into America if he wins.

El-Sayed has criticised similar remarks by Trump as Islamophobic, saying in an ad to voters last week that the US president "thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor's office".

In Port Huron on Sunday, Minaj, wearing a gold-coloured Gucci-branded suit, led the crowd in chanting Trump's name, and the names of Republican candidates in Michigan.

"We really need all these great people to be elected, because this is a major turning point for our country," she said.

"She never looked more beautiful," Trump said as she left the stage. "She gets it. She's smart," he added.

Earlier in his speech, Trump praised the rear end of one male Republican candidate before turning the crowd's attention to Minaj.

"By the way, I looked at a beautiful ass before," he segued. "Nicki Minaj. That's hard to miss."

He then asked her to "stand up" as the crowd cheered, and added that he hoped she was not "insulted" by his remark.

The Super Bass singer had accompanied Trump to the state aboard Air Force One. She filmed a video with an aide - which was posted to X -on the president's plane, pretending to be interviewing for the White House press secretary role.

The position is currently open after Katie Zacharia left five days after a shaky public debut.

The Trinidad and Tobago-born rapper has thrown her star power behind Trump a few times before, including on his allegations that Christians face persecution in Nigeria and his "gold card" visa, which offers applicants residency and a path to US citizenship.

articles.title: Tillis says it’s ‘appropriate to take a look at’ Alaska ballot with two Dan Sullivans running
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) on Sunday said it was “appropriate to take a look at” the outcome of the Alaska Senate race with two candidates with similar names on the ballot, which prompted a Department of Justice (DOJ) lawsuit. “Alaska has a candidate who just coincidentally happens to be the same name as my friend…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) on Sunday said it was “appropriate to take a look at” the outcome of the Alaska Senate race with two candidates with similar names on the ballot, which prompted a Department of Justice (DOJ) lawsuit .

“Alaska has a candidate who just coincidentally happens to be the same name as my friend and colleague who came in with me in 2014,” Tillis told “Face the Nation” host Margaret Brennan on CBS News, referring to Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska). “So I think it’s appropriate to take a look at it.”

Tillis said he was “not sure” why the DOJ had to file a lawsuit “other than, as [Attorney General Todd Blanche] said earlier, make sure that you have the ballots right so we can be certain that the Democrats were not successful in confusing” voters and “better position” Democrat Mary Peltola to be the winner.

Brennan raised the comments made by Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who said the DOJ should not have filed its lawsuit and that “when it came to the ballot, Alaskans don’t need help,” and asked if there will be consequences from Capitol Hill.

“Well, there are very few people that know Alaska better than Lisa, to be honest with you,” Tillis said. “Lisa Murkowski is a friend and an extraordinary member of the U.S. Senate. I agree that –– filing the lawsuit before anything that could be substantiated … It’s almost a preemptive, a presumptive posture, versus simply telling the Alaska election officials, ‘We’re going to be watching this closely.'”

Tillis accused Democrats of “gaming the system” with Daniel J. Sullivan’s name appearing on the ballot.

In Alaska, the top four vote-getters in the primary advance to the general election, which is tabulated using ranked-choice voting. While they have similar names, Sen. Sullivan and Daniel J. Sullivan will appear differently on the ballot , with the senator labeled “incumbent” and “Republican.”

The DOJ filed the suit last Thursday, claiming that the existence of a candidate with a name similar to Sullivan’s would make a win by Peltola invalid.

Blanche, who appeared earlier in the program, told Brennan in a fiery exchange that the DOJ was “asking the court to step in where the Alaska Supreme Court didn’t, which is to look at federal law and, if necessary, to allow a process for Alaska to decide who should be certified as a winner.”

“All we were doing is trying to put guardrails in place so that if that happens, there’s a system allowed where the ballots are kept in a way so that we can determine whether there was confusion,” Blanche said. “It’s not saying, ‘Don’t certify.'”

Blanche would not say whether President Trump directed him to file the lawsuit and denied that the president said, on camera, that he directed the DOJ to file the lawsuit. Trump told reporters on Friday that he had greenlit the preemptive election challenge himself.

“I’m the one who said, ‘Do it,'” Trump said.
